self_review.description: The human-likeness half of write→check→fix. The deterministic checker catches the mechanizable tells; these are the texture checks it cannot verify. The calling model runs each against its OWN draft, rates it, and rewrites every weak spot before returning. Surfaced as the check_text report's manual_review list and sequenced by next_action. Edit here and git-push to update; the server makes no API call.
items: AR-001 — meaning preserved: confirm claims, numbers, names, and stance are unchanged from the source, and the tone the user asked for is intact.

Rhythm: read the draft in your head — do sentence lengths and shapes vary, or march at one cadence? Break up runs of same-length sentences; add a short fragment or a longer multi-clause sentence. (Burstiness is auto-measured; this is the qualitative read.)

Reused rhetorical shape: the same construction — an antithesis ('not X, but Y'), a copula maxim, a rule-of-three — restated across the piece reads as a tic even when the words differ. Vary the constructions, not just the vocabulary.

Section-to-section variation: does the style shift between sections, or hold one flat fingerprint throughout? Humans modulate; LLMs stay even. Make one section terse and another more flowing. (Cross-section uniformity is auto-detected; this is the qualitative read.)

Generic competence and stance: could this have been written about almost any topic, by almost anyone? Cut smooth-but-empty phrasing, reflexive hedges, and motivational closers. Commit to a real point of view and at least one concrete, specific, checkable detail.

Abstraction-as-agent: an abstract noun ('the gap', 'the work', 'the craft', 'the order') used as the subject of an agentive or experiential verb (mattered, decided, kept, taught, carries, carried, holds, demands) reads fluent but no one is actually doing anything. Metaphorical 'carry' is the most frequent instance and the hardest to hear ('the layout carries the weight', 'the silence carried the room', 'eight words to carry'): the verb performs gravity while the sentence names no actor and no effect. Prefer a human or concrete subject, and say what the thing actually does. The fixed collocations are auto-detected as BS-031; the open-ended abstract-subject cases are this rubric item (server cannot verify reliably; see AP-033, AP-044).

Performative framing beat: a sentence or label whose real job is to perform insight, closure, or self-awareness rather than carry content. Three forms — (a) a self-satisfied closer: a neat aphorism ending a section that adds no new fact, name, or number, often crediting the author or pivoting on a tidy antithesis ('The data set is public; the reading of it is mine.'); (b) first-person meta-commentary on the work itself ('my take', 'the reading of it is mine', 'as I see it') in a piece meant to be evidence-led; (c) a clever paradox headline used to sound sharp where a plain statement of the point would do. Delete the beat and end on the last substantive point. Keep at most one aphoristic or paradox construction per piece, and only where it does analytical work — the device is human in moderation; the tell is repetition and substitution for content. The standalone meta-label form ('in 200 words', 'in brief') is auto-detected as BS-022; the closer overlaps BS-018; see AP-035, AP-033.

Excessive coherence and tidiness: does every point line up too neatly — each example fitting perfectly, every thread resolved, no loose ends or tension left? Real human writing has friction: a caveat that complicates the thesis, a digression, an example that only mostly fits, a point left partly open. Seamless, frictionless argument is itself a tell. Add back the messiness the topic actually has.

Durable signal: local word-level unpredictability and section-to-section variation are the most human signals and are not measured server-side. Surface word swaps are necessary but not sufficient — do not stop at vocabulary.
